=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.
exchanges.text:
## Buyer’s position

**Do not accept the Seller’s package as settled.** Its “STANDARD”, “FINAL”, market-practice and prior-agreement statements are Seller assertions, not evidence of Buyer approval. The principal concern is the combination of broad disclosures and knowledge exclusions with limitations applying to **all Claims**: together, these could leave Wattlebridge bearing identified risks without an effective remedy.

This review is based on the supplied update and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying SPA, contracts or DD documents. Those documents and any actual record of agreed positions must be checked before finalising drafting.

## 1. Liability and remedies: preserve meaningful protection

### General warranty cap and thresholds

The AUD 4.8 million cap is correctly calculated as 20% of price, but whether it is acceptable depends on the diligence findings, warranty coverage and available recourse—not the Seller’s “market” label.

The AUD 250,000 basket is **deductible**: only the excess is recoverable. Together with the AUD 25,000 de minimis, it transfers meaningful loss to the Buyer.

**Push back:**
- Seek a lower basket and a **tipping basket**, allowing recovery from the first dollar once crossed.
- Aggregate claims arising from related facts for the de minimis and basket; avoid artificial fragmentation.
- Confirm whether below-de-minimis claims count towards the basket.
- Confine these thresholds and the general cap to ordinary warranty claims, not every contractual remedy.

### Fundamental warranties and time limits

Putting title and capacity under an AUD 4.8 million cap and an 18-month deadline is unacceptable from the Buyer’s perspective. Wattlebridge could pay AUD 24 million but have sharply restricted recovery if the Seller cannot convey valid title.

**Push back:**
- Separate title, capacity, authority and share-encumbrance warranties, with a price-level cap at minimum, no basket/de minimis and a materially longer claim period.
- Give tax claims a separate regime aligned with applicable assessment periods and a reasonable notification buffer.
- Assess IP protection separately, particularly given Ironquay.
- Extend the general warranty notification period—seek at least 24 months, subject to the reporting cycle and diligence findings.
- Ensure timely notified claims survive until resolved. Reject unreasonable notice-detail requirements or short proceedings deadlines that extinguish otherwise valid claims.

### “All Claims” limitations, non-reliance and exclusive remedies

Clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 could undermine specific indemnities, completion obligations, debt repayment and price adjustments—not merely warranty claims.

**Push back:** replace blanket application with an explicit allocation of which limitations apply to each claim category. Preserve:
- Price adjustments, payment obligations and completion deliverables.
- Specific indemnities on their separately negotiated terms.
- Fraud and deliberate concealment carve-outs, with appropriate attribution.
- Injunctive relief and specific performance.
- Rights that cannot lawfully be excluded.

Review the non-reliance language carefully so it does not negate express warranties or agreed disclosures. Do not assume every attempted statutory exclusion is effective under NSW/Australian law.

## 2. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: reject blanket risk transfer

General disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room, accounts and public registers is too broad. It can qualify warranties through obscure references, incomplete documents or material not actually provided.

Clause 8.3 goes further: anything **discoverable** by the Buyer or its advisers could defeat a claim. That effectively turns diligence into a Seller defence.

**Push back:**
- Require fair disclosure in sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the relevant matter, preferably against the relevant warranty.
- Reject blanket public-register disclosure, or restrict it to precisely identified searches and documents.
- Fix and retain an indexed, accessible copy of the disclosed data room at the agreed cutoff.
- Delete constructive/imputed knowledge and “discoverable” knowledge. Prefer no knowledge exclusion; if unavoidable, limit it to actual knowledge of named Buyer personnel concerning the specific breach.
- Ensure disclosure and Buyer knowledge do **not** defeat expressly negotiated specific indemnities.

The Seller cannot both disclose a known problem and use that disclosure to neutralise the protection intended to address it.

## 3. Completion blockers and financial leakage

| Issue | Buyer risk and recommended response |
|---|---|
| **Bluefen — approximately 30% of FY26 revenue** | This is a material customer dependency. No final consent or satisfaction of associated conditions is evidenced. Require a completion condition covering valid consent **and satisfaction of clause 11.3 conditions**, without materially adverse amendments, fees or termination rights unless Buyer-approved. Reasonable endeavours alone is not the required outcome. Include a longstop and Buyer termination right; do not deem the condition satisfied merely on delivery of a consent document. |
| **Riverlark — approximately AUD 3.2 million** | A post-completion release leaves the acquired business exposed to debt, security and enforcement risk. Require a current payout letter and coordinated repayment and effective security releases at Completion, with registrations discharged promptly under binding arrangements. Reflect repayment in the debt-free/cash-free funds flow **without double counting** the debt adjustment. A later release promise is insufficient. |
| **Completion bonuses — AUD 420,000 plus possible on-costs** | Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the Company becoming liable. Verify the employment and Completion conditions, payer, timing, payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs. Allocate Seller transaction-related amounts expressly through transaction expenses/debt-like items, a price deduction or Seller payment, and itemise them in the funds flow. Avoid double counting through working capital. The gross exposure remains unconfirmed. |

## 4. Known operational risks need tailored solutions

### Ironquay IP

The record identifies an **unresolved payment/title issue**, not conclusively proven non-payment. Nevertheless, clause 7.3 makes transfer conditional on all SOW3 fees clearing, and neither payment evidence nor a confirmatory assignment is available.

An indemnity confined to the SOW3 payment may not cover lack of ownership, third-party claims, remediation or business disruption.

**Require:** reconciliation and reliable payment evidence; an effective assignment/confirmation covering the relevant rights and chain of title; and, if unresolved, a specific indemnity covering resulting loss and reasonable remediation costs—not merely the AUD 180,000 balance. Material core-IP defects should be cured before Completion, rather than left solely to damages.

### Export/privacy incident

The Seller’s “not expected to be material” conclusion is unsupported by the preliminary record. Conversely, the documents do **not** establish access, a confirmed notifiable breach or a quantified loss.

**Require:**
- An updated investigation into access, scope, containment and affected data.
- Preservation of evidence and assessment of applicable privacy, contractual and notification obligations.
- Buyer consultation on material investigation and response decisions, without delaying legally required action.
- Appropriate pre-completion covenants and a specific indemnity for consequences of the pre-completion incident, with lawful scope, suitable survival and no general-disclosure defence.

Consider a holdback if material exposure remains unresolved. Assess any completion condition against the actual severity found.

### Sandbar renewals — AUD 330,000 aggregate

Neither “ordinary course” nor “debt-like” treatment is established. Read DD-008 and DD-011 together and determine execution dates, service periods, cancellation rights, accruals and whether these are related commitments.

**Push back:** prohibit material related commitments outside agreed ordinary-course limits without Buyer consent. Allocate amounts according to their economic character: pre-completion accruals, abnormal commitments and post-completion services may require different treatment. Do not automatically deduct all AUD 330,000 or accept the Seller’s blanket characterisation.

## 5. Other diligence points

- **Office lease:** the evidence identifies a notification obligation, not landlord consent. Confirm and satisfy its timing and form; investigate consequences of non-compliance without inventing a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not, by itself, establish that a share sale requires consent. Review the full contract for separate change-of-control provisions.
- **Share title:** DD-012 is relevant evidence, not complete verification. Reconcile the register with the constitution, certificates, issue/transfer history, options and other equity rights; investigate encumbrances and beneficial interests. Require effective transfer deliverables and warranties covering all issued shares and outstanding equity rights.
- **Currency:** the disclosure record is dated 22 September 2026. Require updates through signing and Completion. New disclosures should not automatically qualify warranties or remove Buyer remedies.

## Recommended negotiation priorities

1. **Secure completion essentials:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment/security release, valid share title and resolution of material IP ownership gaps.
2. **Correct the economics:** expressly allocate bonuses and on-costs; verify debt and renewals; produce a reconciled funds flow.
3. **Protect known risks:** tailored Ironquay and incident protections, supported where necessary by retention, escrow or other credit support.
4. **Rebuild the liability framework:** separate general warranties, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities and payment/completion obligations.
5. **Narrow disclosure and knowledge exclusions:** reject blanket data-room and constructive-knowledge defences.

**Bottom line:** negotiate the package as an allocation of actual risks, not as a collection of purportedly “standard” clauses. Disclosure identifies problems; it does not resolve them or justify shifting their cost to Wattlebridge.
